explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Amaziah, king of Judah, says, “Come, let us meet face to face…” (2 Chronicles 25:17). Sounds friendly, doesn't it? I think a message like that could mean a lot of things, and the next verses show it wasn't a friendly chat.

No treaty in this message, baker. Amaziah, king of Judah, just says, “Come, let us meet face to face…” (2 Chronicles 25:17). He doesn't mention a deal or a signing. It's a short invitation, nothing more.

Not that one, friend. Amaziah asks for no silver and no gold. He only says, “Come, let us meet face to face…” (2 Chronicles 25:17). The gold does change hands later, but it leaves Jerusalem, and that's not a good day for Judah.

Yes, baker. Jehoash, king of Israel, says, “Then a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle.” (2 Chronicles 25:18). Short story, and the ending is rough on the thistle. That thistle went in asking for a wedding and came out flat.
Good guess, but that's not how Jehoash tells it. The text says a wild beast came along and trampled the thistle (2 Chronicles 25:18). The beast does the trampling, not the cedar.

No wind in this one, friend. Jehoash, king of Israel, says a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle (2 Chronicles 25:18). Uprooting is a gentler ending than stomping, and the thistle doesn't get the gentle one.

True, baker. Jehoash says, “You have said, ‘Look, I have defeated Edom,’ and your heart has become proud and boastful.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). He doesn't dance around it. He repeats Amaziah's own words about Edom and then says his heart has become proud and boastful.

It's true, friend. Jehoash tells Amaziah, “…your heart has become proud and boastful.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). He says it right after repeating Amaziah's own words about defeating Edom. No hint-dropping here. He says it plainly in his reply.
Home it is, baker. Jehoash says, “Now stay at home.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). Four words and a whole lot of sense. I stayed put in a junk drawer for years, so trust me, it can be done.
Not armed, friend. Jehoash says, “Now stay at home.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). He isn't telling Amaziah to gear up. He's telling him to sit tight and stay put.
Watchful sounds wise, but that's not the word. Jehoash says, “Now stay at home.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). It's a plain instruction with no extra instructions attached. Just stay where you are, baker.

Careful with this one, baker. Jehoash asks, “Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall—you and Judah with you?” (2 Chronicles 25:19). Judah falls right alongside Amaziah. The warning covers both of them, so the statement is false.

Right, baker. Jehoash says, “Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall—you and Judah with you?” (2 Chronicles 25:19). Amaziah isn't the only one in that warning, because Judah is named right alongside him. That's the part that stings.

explanations.answer: They had sought the gods of Edom
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. The writer says this had come from God “…because they had sought the gods of Edom.” (2 Chronicles 25:20). Edom, the nation Amaziah says he defeated, had gods of its own, and Judah went looking to them. The text gives the reason plainly, so I won't add one.

explanations.answer: They had broken a treaty with Israel
explanations.explanation: No treaty in the text, friend. The writer says this had come from God “…because they had sought the gods of Edom.” (2 Chronicles 25:20). That's the only reason given. I'm not going to invent one for the writer.

explanations.answer: They had ignored the Sabbath day
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the Sabbath here, baker. The writer says it plainly: “…because they had sought the gods of Edom.” (2 Chronicles 25:20). Edom was the nation Judah had just defeated. That's the reason the text gives, and it gives no other.

explanations.answer: They all scatter and run away
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says Judah “…was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his own home.” (2 Chronicles 25:22). Every man heads for his own front door. I think that's what happens when the plan falls apart and nobody wants to be the last one standing.

No surrender in this verse, friend. It says Judah “…was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his own home.” (2 Chronicles 25:22). They didn't line up and hand anything over. They ran, each man to his own home.

Nobody regroups here, baker. The text says Judah “…was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his own home.” (2 Chronicles 25:22). Each man goes to his own home, not to a meeting point. It's less of a plan and more of a scramble.

Not this time, baker. The text says, “There at Beth-shemesh, Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah…” (2 Chronicles 25:23). Amaziah never gets away. He's caught right there on the battlefield, so the statement is false.

Right, baker. Jehoash captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, and the text says it happened “There at Beth-shemesh…” (2 Chronicles 25:23). The army scatters, but Amaziah is captured. He asked for a face to face meeting, and he got one.

explanations.answer: Breaks down a long section of it
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jehoash “…broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—a section of four hundred cubits.” (2 Chronicles 25:23). That's a big stretch of wall, and it's Jerusalem's own wall. A city feels that one.

explanations.answer: Sets his guards all along it
explanations.explanation: Not guards, friend. The text says Jehoash “…broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—a section of four hundred cubits.” (2 Chronicles 25:23). He breaks the wall down, and the text never mentions guards.

Not all of it stays standing, baker. Jehoash “…broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—a section of four hundred cubits.” (2 Chronicles 25:23). It isn't the whole wall, but it's a big section, and it comes down.

Hostages, baker. The text says Jehoash took the gold, the silver and the articles, “…as well as some hostages.” (2 Chronicles 25:24). Then he returned to Samaria. He took treasure from the house of God and the royal palace treasuries, and people went with him too.

Not horses, friend. The text says Jehoash took the treasure “…as well as some hostages.” (2 Chronicles 25:24). Horses do show up later in the passage, but only to carry Amaziah's body back (2 Chronicles 25:28). Here, it's people he takes.

Close in feeling, but no, baker. The text says Jehoash took the treasure “…as well as some hostages.” (2 Chronicles 25:24). It doesn't name priests or anyone else in particular. I won't add details the text leaves out.
Lachish, baker. The text says Amaziah “…fled to Lachish.” (2 Chronicles 25:27). He runs there with a conspiracy behind him. The men sent after him still find him there.
Not Hebron, friend. The text says that after the conspiracy formed, Amaziah “…fled to Lachish.” (2 Chronicles 25:27). Lachish is where he runs. That's also where the men sent after him catch up.

Not Bethel, baker. Amaziah “…fled to Lachish.” (2 Chronicles 25:27). A conspiracy had been formed against him in Jerusalem, and the men sent after him still reach him there. It's a quiet, heavy part of the story.
